 35 |     watch_category            VARCHAR(15)    NOT NULL

 37 | GO
 38 | CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE rpt.usp_large_loss_watchlist
 39 |     @AsOfDate DATE
 40 | AS
 41 | BEGIN
 42 |     SET NOCOUNT ON;
 43 | 
 44 |     DECLARE @job       VARCHAR(128) = 'rpt.usp_large_loss_watchlist';
 45 |     DECLARE @PriorDate DATE         = DATEADD(DAY, -90, @AsOfDate);
 46 |     DECLARE @rows      INT;
 47 | 
 48 |     BEGIN TRY
 49 |         EXEC etl.usp_log_step @job_name = @job, @step_name = 'start', @status = 'STARTED';
 50 | 
 51 |         -- open and reopened claims, plus claims closed in the last 90 days
 52 |         SELECT c.claim_id, c.claim_number, c.policy_id,
 53 |                UPPER(LTRIM(RTRIM(c.lob_code))) AS lob_code,
 54 |                UPPER(LTRIM(RTRIM(c.status)))   AS claim_status,
 55 |                c.reported_date, c.closed_date
 56 |         INTO #clm
 57 |         FROM stg.claims c WITH (NOLOCK)
 58 |         WHERE c.reported_date <= @AsOfDate
 59 |           AND (c.status <> 'CLOSED' OR c.closed_date > @PriorDate);
 60 |         SET @rows = @@ROWCOUNT;
 61 |         EXEC etl.usp_log_step @job_name = @job, @step_name = 'claims', @status = 'INFO', @rows_affected = @rows;
 62 | 
 63 |         -- payments to date and 90 days ago; unkeyed amounts count as nil
 64 |         SELECT p.claim_id,
 65 |                SUM(ISNULL(p.amount, 0)) AS paid_now,
 66 |                SUM(CASE WHEN p.payment_date <= @PriorDate THEN ISNULL(p.amount, 0) ELSE 0 END) AS paid_prior,
 67 |                MAX(CASE WHEN p.amount IS NOT NULL THEN p.payment_date END) AS last_payment_date
 68 |         INTO #paid
 69 |         FROM stg.claim_payments p WITH (NOLOCK)
 70 |         INNER JOIN #clm c ON c.claim_id = p.claim_id
 71 |         WHERE p.payment_date <= @AsOfDate
 72 |         GROUP BY p.claim_id;
 73 | 
 74 |         -- outstanding reserve as at today and 90 days ago
 75 |         SELECT r.claim_id, d.period, r.reserve_amount,
 76 |                ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY d.period, r.claim_id
 77 |                                   ORDER BY r.reserve_date DESC, r.reserve_id DESC) AS rn
 78 |         INTO #res
 79 |         FROM stg.claim_reserves r WITH (NOLOCK)
 80 |         INNER JOIN #clm c ON c.claim_id = r.claim_id
 81 |         CROSS APPLY (VALUES ('NOW', @AsOfDate), ('PRIOR', @PriorDate)) d (period, as_at)
 82 |         WHERE r.reserve_date <= d.as_at;
 83 | 
 84 |         SELECT claim_id,
 85 |                SUM(CASE WHEN period = 'NOW'   THEN reserve_amount ELSE 0 END) AS os_now,
 86 |                SUM(CASE WHEN period = 'PRIOR' THEN reserve_amount ELSE 0 END) AS os_prior
 87 |         INTO #os
 88 |         FROM #res
 89 |         WHERE rn = 1
 90 |         GROUP BY claim_id;
 91 | 
 92 |         -- reserve activity
 93 |         SELECT r.claim_id,
 94 |                SUM(CASE WHEN r.reserve_date > @PriorDate THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS reserve_changes_90d,
 95 |                MAX(r.reserve_date) AS last_reserve_date
 96 |         INTO #ract
 97 |         FROM stg.claim_reserves r WITH (NOLOCK)
 98 |         INNER JOIN #clm c ON c.claim_id = r.claim_id
 99 |         WHERE r.reserve_date <= @AsOfDate
100 |         GROUP BY r.claim_id;
101 | 
102 |         SELECT c.claim_id,
103 |                ISNULL(p.paid_now, 0) AS paid_to_date,
104 |                ISNULL(o.os_now, 0) AS outstanding_reserve,
105 |                ISNULL(p.paid_now, 0) + ISNULL(o.os_now, 0) AS incurred_amount,
106 |                ISNULL(p.paid_prior, 0) + ISNULL(o.os_prior, 0) AS incurred_90d_ago,
107 |                ISNULL(a.reserve_changes_90d, 0) AS reserve_changes_90d,
108 |                CASE WHEN ISNULL(p.last_payment_date, '19000101') > ISNULL(a.last_reserve_date, '19000101')
109 |                     THEN p.last_payment_date ELSE a.last_reserve_date END AS last_activity_date
110 |         INTO #inc
111 |         FROM #clm c
112 |         LEFT JOIN #paid p ON p.claim_id = c.claim_id
113 |         LEFT JOIN #os o   ON o.claim_id = c.claim_id
114 |         LEFT JOIN #ract a ON a.claim_id = c.claim_id;
115 | 
116 |         TRUNCATE TABLE rpt.large_loss_watchlist;
117 | 
118 |         INSERT INTO rpt.large_loss_watchlist
119 |             (as_of_date, claim_id, claim_number, policy_id, lob_code, claim_status, reported_date,
120 |              closed_date, paid_to_date, outstanding_reserve, incurred_amount, incurred_90d_ago,
121 |              movement_90d, reserve_changes_90d, days_since_last_activity, watch_category)
122 |         SELECT @AsOfDate, c.claim_id, c.claim_number, c.policy_id, c.lob_code, c.claim_status,
123 |                c.reported_date, c.closed_date,
124 |                i.paid_to_date, i.outstanding_reserve, i.incurred_amount, i.incurred_90d_ago,
125 |                i.incurred_amount - i.incurred_90d_ago,
126 |                i.reserve_changes_90d,
127 |                DATEDIFF(DAY, i.last_activity_date, @AsOfDate),
128 |                CASE WHEN i.incurred_90d_ago < 25000 THEN 'NEW'
129 |                     WHEN i.incurred_amount > i.incurred_90d_ago * 1.10 THEN 'DETERIORATING'
130 |                     WHEN i.incurred_amount < i.incurred_90d_ago * 0.90 THEN 'IMPROVING'
131 |                     ELSE 'STABLE' END
132 |         FROM #inc i
133 |         INNER JOIN #clm c ON c.claim_id = i.claim_id
134 |         WHERE i.incurred_amount >= 25000;
135 |         SET @rows = @@ROWCOUNT;
136 |         EXEC etl.usp_log_step @job_name = @job, @step_name = 'load rpt.large_loss_watchlist', @status = 'INFO', @rows_affected = @rows;
137 | 
138 |         EXEC etl.usp_log_step @job_name = @job, @step_name = 'end', @status = 'SUCCESS';
139 |     END TRY
140 |     BEGIN CATCH
141 |         DECLARE @msg NVARCHAR(4000) = ERROR_MESSAGE(), @err INT = ERROR_NUMBER();
142 |         EXEC etl.usp_log_step @job_name = @job, @step_name = 'end', @status = 'FAILED',
143 |              @message = @msg, @error_number = @err;
144 |         THROW;
145 |     END CATCH
146 | END;
147 | GO

Trap findings in this job:
- TSQL-13 lines 56-56: Temp table #clm holds the filtered claims; it becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-01 lines 59-59: c.status is VARCHAR(12) and is compared before the trim and upper-case. Under the CI collation, 'Closed' and 'closed' count as CLOSED and are dropped once closed more than 90 days ago. Spark's binary <> would keep them.
- TSQL-02 lines 59-59: The raw status is compared untrimmed. SQL Server treats 'CLOSED ' as equal to 'CLOSED', but Spark does not, so old closed claims padded with trailing spaces would stay in the Spark result.
- TSQL-13 lines 68-68: Temp table #paid holds the payment aggregates; it becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-13 lines 78-78: Temp table #res holds the reserve rows ranked per period; it becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-09 lines 81-82: CROSS APPLY (VALUES ...) multiplies each reserve row into a NOW and a PRIOR period. Spark has no APPLY, so this becomes a cross join with a two-row DataFrame, followed by the reserve_date <= as_at filter.
- TSQL-13 lines 87-87: Temp table #os holds the outstanding reserves now and 90 days ago; it becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-13 lines 96-96: Temp table #ract holds the reserve activity; it becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-06 lines 108-109: ISNULL takes the DATE type of its first argument, so '19000101' becomes the date 1900-01-01. In Spark, coalesce(date, '19000101') widens to string or fails to cast that literal, so the replacement must be written as a typed date literal.
- TSQL-13 lines 110-110: Temp table #inc holds the incurred amounts; it becomes a DataFrame.
- TSQL-04 lines 127-127: DATEDIFF(DAY, start, end) on DATE values gives the day difference. Spark's datediff takes its arguments in reverse order (end, start), so they must be swapped to avoid a negated result.
- TSQL-07 lines 129-130: incurred_90d_ago * 1.10 and * 0.90 are exact DECIMAL multiplications in T-SQL. In PySpark, F.lit(1.10) is a double, which can put a claim on the boundary into the wrong DETERIORATING/IMPROVING/STABLE category. Use decimal literals.

Trap cards:
### TSQL-01 (semantic): Case-insensitive collation in =, IN, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, PARTITION BY and joins
Legacy: Under a case-insensitive collation such as SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS, text compares equal regardless of letter case (and of trailing spaces, see TSQL-02): state = 'ACTIVE' also matches 'Active' and 'active'; GROUP BY, DISTINCT, PARTITION BY and join keys put case variants together. The stored value is returned unchanged.
Spark: Spark compares strings in binary order: 'Active' <> 'ACTIVE', so a filter drops case variants, a GROUP BY splits them into separate groups and a join misses them.
Fix: Compare, group, partition and join on upper(rtrim(x)) (or collate(x, 'UTF8_LCASE_RTRIM')) while selecting the original column for output. Never change the stored value unless the legacy code does (e.g. UPPER in the SELECT). Use rtrim, not trim: leading spaces count.
Example: WHERE o.order_state IN ('SHIPPED', 'BILLED') -> F.upper(F.rtrim('order_state')).isin('SHIPPED', 'BILLED')

### TSQL-02 (semantic): Comparisons ignore trailing spaces; CHAR(n) pads with spaces
Legacy: SQL Server pads the shorter string with spaces before comparing, so 'WEST ' = 'WEST' (also in IN, GROUP BY and joins). CHAR(n) and NCHAR(n) values are stored and returned padded to n characters: 'AB' in a CHAR(4) column is 'AB '. LEN() ignores trailing spaces (TSQL-15). Leading spaces always count.
Spark: Spark compares strings exactly, so 'WEST ' <> 'WEST', and its string type never pads. A value read from a CHAR source column keeps whatever spaces it was stored with.
Fix: rtrim both sides of every text comparison, grouping and join key. Where the legacy output column is CHAR(n)/NCHAR(n), pad the value with rpad(x, n, ' ') (NULL stays NULL) so the output matches the stored legacy value. A CHAR(n) source column read into an expression keeps its padding (e.g. in + concatenation).
Example: account_type CHAR(4) ... WHERE region = 'WEST' -> F.rpad('account_type', 4, ' ') ... F.rtrim('region') == 'WEST'

### TSQL-04 (semantic): DATEDIFF counts boundaries crossed, not elapsed periods
Legacy: DATEDIFF(datepart, a, b) counts the datepart boundaries crossed between a and b: DATEDIFF(year, '2025-12-31', '2026-01-01') = 1 and DATEDIFF(month, '2025-01-31', '2025-02-01') = 1. DATEDIFF(week, ...) counts Sundays crossed, whatever SET DATEFIRST says. DATEDIFF(day, ...) on DATE values equals the day difference.
Spark: datediff(end, start) counts days (arguments reversed); months_between returns a fraction with its own month-end rule; floor(months/12) counts elapsed years, not boundaries.
Fix: year: year(b) - year(a). quarter: (year(b)*4 + quarter(b)) - (year(a)*4 + quarter(a)). month: (year(b)*12 + month(b)) - (year(a)*12 + month(a)). week: the difference of Sunday-anchored week numbers, floor(datediff(x, DATE'1899-12-31') / 7) for b minus a. day: datediff(b, a). Mind the argument order: T-SQL is (part, start, end), Spark's datediff is (end, start).
Example: DATEDIFF(YEAR, e.hire_date, @AsOfDate) -> F.year(as_of) - F.year('hire_date')

### TSQL-06 (semantic): ISNULL takes the type of its first argument; NULL treated as equal in change checks
Legacy: ISNULL(a, b) returns a's data type, so the replacement b is converted to it: a VARCHAR(5) column with ISNULL(col, 'UNKNOWN') returns 'UNKNO' (truncated), and ISNULL(int_col, 0.5) returns 0. COALESCE uses the highest-precedence type instead. Change detection written as ISNULL(src, '') <> ISNULL(tgt, '') treats NULL and '' as the same value.
Spark: coalesce() keeps the replacement as written ('UNKNOWN') and widens types; it never truncates.
Fix: Translate ISNULL(a, b) to coalesce(a, b) cast to a's type: for character types, truncate b to a's declared length with substring(b, 1, n) (look the length up in the input DDL); for integer a, cast b to the integer type. In change detection, reproduce the NULL-equals-'' semantics with coalesce(x, '') on both sides.
Example: ISNULL(o.channel_code, 'UNASSIGNED')   -- channel_code VARCHAR(8) -> F.coalesce('channel_code', F.lit('UNASSIGNED').substr(1, 8))

### TSQL-07 (semantic): DECIMAL precision and scale, and ROUND on computed values
Legacy: DECIMAL arithmetic follows fixed precision and scale rules (e.g. division keeps at least 6 decimal places, results are capped at 38 digits and the scale shrinks to fit); intermediate results are rounded at each step to their result type. ROUND(x, n) rounds half away from zero; ROUND(x, n, 1) truncates. Assigning to a DECIMAL(p,s) column rounds.
Spark: Spark's decimal rules are similar but not identical (scale reduction, and doubles if an operand is a double literal); F.round on a double rounds the binary value, so a computed 2.675 (really 2.67499...) rounds to 2.67; bround is half-even.
Fix: Keep computations in decimal: cast operands to the legacy DECIMAL types first, cast each intermediate result to the type T-SQL would give it, and round with F.round on decimals (half up). For ROUND(x, n, 1) use truncation: floor/ceil toward zero at n places. Never introduce doubles where the legacy used DECIMAL.
Example: ROUND(o.net_amount * o.tax_rate, 2) -> F.round((F.col('net_amount') * F.col('tax_rate')).cast('decimal(38,6)'), 2)

### TSQL-09 (construct): CROSS APPLY / OUTER APPLY with TOP 1
Legacy: CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 ... WHERE inner.k = outer.k ORDER BY ...) picks one inner row per outer row and drops outer rows with no match; OUTER APPLY keeps them with NULLs.
Spark: Spark has no APPLY; a lateral subquery or a window replaces it.
Fix: Join on the correlation condition, rank the matches with row_number() over (partition by the outer row's key, order by the APPLY's ORDER BY plus a unique tiebreaker) and keep rank 1; inner join for CROSS APPLY, left join for OUTER APPLY.
Example: CROSS APPLY (SELECT TOP 1 p.price FROM price_history p WHERE p.item_id = o.item_id AND p.valid_from <= o.order_date ORDER BY p.valid_from DESC) px -> row_number() over (partition by order_id order by valid_from desc) = 1 after a join on item_id and valid_from <= order_date

### TSQL-13 (construct): Temp tables
Legacy: #temp tables hold intermediate results for the session.
Spark: Intermediate results are DataFrames or temporary views.
Fix: Make each #temp table a DataFrame (or temp view). Keep its column types: SELECT INTO creates columns with the source expressions' types, which can matter downstream.
Example: SELECT ... INTO #active_orders FROM dbo.orders -> active_orders = orders.where(...)

The ROW_NUMBER at lines 76-77 groups by (period, claim_id) only, not by reserve_type. So each claim keeps just its single latest reserve row, whatever its type. The header says expense reserves count towards incurred (CR-0577), but they are only included when the expense reserve happens to be the latest row. The SUM at lines 85-86 then always adds up exactly one row per period. The PySpark version must copy this exactly, not fix it. Ties on reserve_date are broken by reserve_id DESC.

When computing last_payment_date, payments with a NULL amount are skipped (line 67), but they still count as nil in the sums.

days_since_last_activity is NULL when the claim has no payments and no reserves. The 1900-01-01 sentinel only affects the comparison and never reaches the output.

The filter edges on payment_date, reserve_date and the claim_id joins in the payment and reserve steps decide which payment and reserve rows feed the sums. They change which rows appear only indirectly, through the incurred_amount >= 25000 threshold at line 134.

Suspected legacy bugs found at Design (reproduce each exactly, and mark the lines that reproduce it with the marker and its id):

That leaves one reserve row per claim and period. A claim usually holds an indemnity reserve and an expense reserve (CR-0577). Only the most recently changed of the two goes into outstanding_reserve, and the other type's open reserve is dropped. This understates outstanding_reserve, incurred_amount, incurred_90d_ago and movement_90d. It can also keep claims off the list entirely or give them the wrong watch_category.
- X2-D2 Claims closed exactly 90 days ago are dropped (lines [11, 45, 59]): The claim filter keeps closed claims only when closed_date > @PriorDate, where @PriorDate is AsOfDate - 90 days (2025-10-02). A claim closed on 2025-10-02, exactly 90 days before the as-of date, is therefore left out.
- X2-D3 CLOSED check uses the raw status, not the trimmed one (lines [14, 54, 59]): Line 59 compares the untrimmed c.status with 'CLOSED'. SQL Server ignores trailing spaces and, under the usual collation, case, but it does not ignore leading spaces. A status such as ' CLOSED' passes the <> 'CLOSED' test, so claims closed long ago (or with no closed_date) still make the list. They then appear as 'CLOSED' because the output column is trimmed (INC-3204).

"""X2 usp_large_loss_watchlist: migrated from estate/holdout/X2_usp_large_loss_watchlist.sql.

Legacy SHA-256: bc9df85f8e39e93cc102c59e14ed2d6f84543a4a3c5cdc8b445ab1108e162772
Written by: LANSH translator (Claude)
Traps handled: TSQL-01, TSQL-02, TSQL-04, TSQL-06, TSQL-07, TSQL-09, TSQL-13
Bugs reproduced on purpose (# LANSH-DEFECT): X2-D1 latest reserve picked across all reserve types; X2-D2 claims closed exactly 90 days ago dropped; X2-D3 CLOSED check uses the raw (untrimmed-left) status
"""
import datetime
from decimal import Decimal

from pyspark.sql import DataFrame, SparkSession, Window
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql import types as T


def run(spark: SparkSession, inputs: dict[str, DataFrame], params: dict[str, str]) -> dict[str, DataFrame]:
    claims = inputs["stg.claims"]
    payments = inputs["stg.claim_payments"]
    reserves = inputs["stg.claim_reserves"]

    as_of = datetime.date.fromisoformat(params["AsOfDate"])
    prior = as_of - datetime.timedelta(days=90)  # DATEADD(DAY, -90, @AsOfDate)
    as_of_lit = F.lit(as_of)
    prior_lit = F.lit(prior)

    # TSQL-13: #clm -> DataFrame
    # TSQL-01 / TSQL-02: status compared case-insensitively and ignoring trailing spaces only
    clm = (
        claims
        .where(
            (F.col("reported_date") <= as_of_lit)
            & (
                (F.upper(F.rtrim(F.col("status"))) != F.lit("CLOSED"))  # LANSH-DEFECT: X2-D3 raw status compared; leading spaces still count so ' CLOSED' passes
                | (F.col("closed_date") > prior_lit)  # LANSH-DEFECT: X2-D2 strict > drops claims closed exactly 90 days ago
            )
        )
        .select(
            F.col("claim_id"),
            F.col("claim_number"),
            F.col("policy_id"),
            F.upper(F.trim(F.col("lob_code"))).alias("lob_code"),
            F.upper(F.trim(F.col("status"))).alias("claim_status"),
            F.col("reported_date"),
            F.col("closed_date"),
        )
    )
    clm_ids = clm.select("claim_id")

    # TSQL-13: #paid -> DataFrame
    zero_12_2 = F.lit(0).cast("decimal(12,2)")
    amt = F.coalesce(F.col("amount"), zero_12_2)  # TSQL-06: ISNULL keeps decimal(12,2)
    paid = (
        payments
        .where(F.col("payment_date") <= as_of_lit)
        .join(clm_ids, on="claim_id", how="inner")
        .groupBy("claim_id")
        .agg(
            F.sum(amt).cast("decimal(38,2)").alias("paid_now"),
            F.sum(F.when(F.col("payment_date") <= prior_lit, amt).otherwise(zero_12_2)).cast("decimal(38,2)").alias("paid_prior"),
            F.max(F.when(F.col("amount").isNotNull(), F.col("payment_date"))).alias("last_payment_date"),
        )
    )

    # TSQL-09: CROSS APPLY (VALUES ...) -> cross join with a two-row DataFrame, then the as_at filter
    periods = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("NOW", as_of), ("PRIOR", prior)],
        T.StructType([
            T.StructField("period", T.StringType(), False),
            T.StructField("as_at", T.DateType(), False),
        ]),
    )
    # TSQL-13: #res -> DataFrame
    w_res = Window.partitionBy("period", "claim_id").orderBy(  # LANSH-DEFECT: X2-D1 partition ignores reserve_type, only the single latest reserve row counts
        F.col("reserve_date").desc(), F.col("reserve_id").desc(), F.col("_row_seq").asc()
    )
    res = (
        reserves
        .join(clm_ids, on="claim_id", how="inner")
        .crossJoin(periods)
        .where(F.col("reserve_date") <= F.col("as_at"))
        .select(
            F.col("claim_id"), F.col("period"), F.col("reserve_amount"),
            F.row_number().over(w_res).alias("rn"),
        )
    )

    # TSQL-13: #os -> DataFrame
    os_df = (
        res
        .where(F.col("rn") == 1)  # LANSH-DEFECT: X2-D1 keeps one reserve row per claim and period, other reserve types dropped
        .groupBy("claim_id")
        .agg(
            F.sum(F.when(F.col("period") == F.lit("NOW"), F.col("reserve_amount")).otherwise(zero_12_2)).cast("decimal(38,2)").alias("os_now"),  # LANSH-DEFECT: X2-D1 sums exactly one row (latest of any type)
            F.sum(F.when(F.col("period") == F.lit("PRIOR"), F.col("reserve_amount")).otherwise(zero_12_2)).cast("decimal(38,2)").alias("os_prior"),  # LANSH-DEFECT: X2-D1 sums exactly one row (latest of any type)
        )
    )

    # TSQL-13: #ract -> DataFrame
    ract = (
        reserves
        .where(F.col("reserve_date") <= as_of_lit)
        .join(clm_ids, on="claim_id", how="inner")
        .groupBy("claim_id")
        .agg(
            F.sum(F.when(F.col("reserve_date") > prior_lit, F.lit(1)).otherwise(F.lit(0))).cast("int").alias("reserve_changes_90d"),
            F.max(F.col("reserve_date")).alias("last_reserve_date"),
        )
    )

    # TSQL-13: #inc -> DataFrame
    zero_38_2 = F.lit(0).cast("decimal(38,2)")
    # TSQL-06: ISNULL(date, '19000101') -> typed date literal
    sentinel = F.to_date(F.lit("19000101"), "yyyyMMdd")
    inc = (
        clm_ids
        .join(paid, on="claim_id", how="left")
        .join(os_df, on="claim_id", how="left")
        .join(ract, on="claim_id", how="left")
        .select(
            F.col("claim_id"),
            F.coalesce(F.col("paid_now"), zero_38_2).alias("paid_to_date"),
            F.coalesce(F.col("os_now"), zero_38_2).alias("outstanding_reserve"),
            (F.coalesce(F.col("paid_now"), zero_38_2) + F.coalesce(F.col("os_now"), zero_38_2)).cast("decimal(38,2)").alias("incurred_amount"),
            (F.coalesce(F.col("paid_prior"), zero_38_2) + F.coalesce(F.col("os_prior"), zero_38_2)).cast("decimal(38,2)").alias("incurred_90d_ago"),
            F.coalesce(F.col("reserve_changes_90d"), F.lit(0).cast("int")).alias("reserve_changes_90d"),
            F.when(
                F.coalesce(F.col("last_payment_date"), sentinel) > F.coalesce(F.col("last_reserve_date"), sentinel),
                F.col("last_payment_date"),
            ).otherwise(F.col("last_reserve_date")).alias("last_activity_date"),
        )
    )

    # TSQL-07: exact decimal multipliers
    up = F.lit(Decimal("1.10"))
    down = F.lit(Decimal("0.90"))
    i_inc = F.col("incurred_amount")
    i_prior = F.col("incurred_90d_ago")

    out = (
        inc
        .join(clm, on="claim_id", how="inner")
        .where(i_inc >= F.lit(25000))
        .select(
            as_of_lit.alias("as_of_date"),
            F.col("claim_id"),
            F.col("claim_number"),
            F.col("policy_id"),
            F.col("lob_code"),
            F.col("claim_status"),
            F.col("reported_date"),
            F.col("closed_date"),
            F.col("paid_to_date"),
            F.col("outstanding_reserve"),
            i_inc.alias("incurred_amount"),
            i_prior.alias("incurred_90d_ago"),
            (i_inc - i_prior).cast("decimal(38,2)").alias("movement_90d"),
            F.col("reserve_changes_90d"),
            # TSQL-04: DATEDIFF(DAY, start, end) -> datediff(end, start)
            F.datediff(as_of_lit, F.col("last_activity_date")).alias("days_since_last_activity"),
            F.when(i_prior < F.lit(25000), F.lit("NEW"))
             .when(i_inc > i_prior * up, F.lit("DETERIORATING"))
             .when(i_inc < i_prior * down, F.lit("IMPROVING"))
             .otherwise(F.lit("STABLE")).alias("watch_category"),
        )
    )

    return {"rpt.large_loss_watchlist": out}

defects.what_it_does: ROW_NUMBER partitions by (period, claim_id) only and keeps rn = 1, so each claim and period has just its single latest reserve row, of any type. The #os sums then add up that one row.

structured_output.notes:
1. Ties in ROW_NUMBER with the same reserve_date and reserve_id are broken by ascending _row_seq. The legacy order is non-deterministic in that case.
2. The joins to #clm are kept as real joins rather than semi-joins, including the final #inc-to-#clm join. Duplicate claim_ids in stg.claims would multiply rows in the same way as in the legacy job.
3. The status filter uses upper(rtrim(status)), which reproduces case-insensitive, trailing-space-insensitive collation while leading spaces still count (X2-D3). LTRIM/RTRIM in the output columns map to F.trim, which trims spaces only.
4. Intermediate sums are cast to decimal(38,2) to match T-SQL's SUM type. The 1.10 and 0.90 multipliers are Decimal literals, so the comparison is exact.
5. The 1900-01-01 sentinel is built from the legacy literal '19000101' as a typed date.
